body.heading: Machines that trade, not create
paragraphs: A simple machine never reduces the total work needed for a job. Instead it trades: less force, applied over a longer distance. A pulley, a ramp and a screw are three classic ways to make that trade, and each is still at work around you every day.

A single pulley fixed overhead simply changes the direction of a pull, letting you haul downward — using your own weight to help — instead of lifting straight up. Add a second, movable pulley and the rope shares the load between two segments, halving the force you need while doubling the rope you must pull.

body.heading: Ramps and screws: slopes in disguise
paragraphs: A ramp spreads a lift over a longer, gentler path. Pushing a heavy box up a long shallow ramp takes far less force than lifting it vertically, because at every moment you are only fighting a small part of its weight. The gentler the slope, the smaller the force — and the longer the journey.

A screw is a ramp wrapped around a cylinder. Turning it many times drives it forward a tiny distance with enormous force, which is why a screw holds so tightly and why a car jack can lift a tonne of car with a handle one person can turn.

body.heading: Simple machines on big jobs
paragraphs: Tower cranes combine pulleys into systems called block and tackle, where many rope segments share the load. With enough segments, a modest motor can raise a steel beam weighing several tonnes — slowly, because all that shared force is paid for in metres of rope hauled through the machine.

Mountain roads are ramps with the same logic. A road that switchbacks up a pass in long zigzags is far longer than the straight climb, but its gentle slope lets an ordinary car engine do what would otherwise be impossible. The pyramids were likely raised the same way: huge stones, modest forces, long ramps.

description: Pulleys share loads, ramps stretch climbs, and a screw is a ramp in disguise — three ancient machines still doing heavy work.
